beginner.json.$comment: Beginner layer: the 'At a glance' strip on compound pages, the summary box's reading time and the technical-details block. Answers are keyed by data values (vocab.ts), so every compound with the same facts gets the same words. Keep every answer to one plain line (B1, everyday words, no jargon).

authorised-elsewhere.text: Approved only in some countries outside the EU.

exenatide-approval.title: Exenatide, a GLP-1 receptor medicine, is approved
exenatide-approval.text: On 28 April 2005 the FDA approved Byetta (exenatide), a synthetic peptide first identified in Gila monster venom. The EU authorised it on 20 November 2006; that authorisation was withdrawn at the company's request on 1 January 2026.

liraglutide-approval.title: Liraglutide: a once-daily GLP-1 medicine
liraglutide-approval.text: The EU authorised Victoza (liraglutide) on 30 June 2009 and the FDA approved it on 25 January 2010. It binds to albumin in the blood and resists breakdown, so one injection a day is enough.

tesamorelin-approval.title: Tesamorelin is approved in the US
tesamorelin-approval.text: On 10 November 2010 the FDA approved Egrifta (tesamorelin), an analogue of growth-hormone-releasing factor, to reduce excess belly fat in adults with HIV and lipodystrophy. An EU application was withdrawn in 2012, and it is not authorised in the EU.

afamelanotide-approval.title: Afamelanotide: authorised under exceptional circumstances
afamelanotide-approval.text: On 22 December 2014 the EU authorised Scenesse (afamelanotide), an implant for a rare disease that makes light painful, under 'exceptional circumstances' because full data could not be collected. The FDA approved it on 8 October 2019.

semaglutide-approval.title: Semaglutide is approved
semaglutide-approval.text: The FDA approved Ozempic (semaglutide) for type 2 diabetes on 5 December 2017, and the EU authorised it on 8 February 2018.

bremelanotide-approval.title: Bremelanotide is approved in the US
bremelanotide-approval.text: On 21 June 2019 the FDA approved Vyleesi (bremelanotide), a melanocortin-receptor agonist, for low sexual desire in some premenopausal women. The EMA lists no application for it, and it is not authorised in the EU.

wegovy-approval.title: Semaglutide for weight management
wegovy-approval.text: The FDA approved Wegovy (semaglutide) for weight management on 4 June 2021, and the EU authorised it on 6 January 2022.

tirzepatide-approval.title: Tirzepatide is approved
tirzepatide-approval.text: The FDA approved Mounjaro (tirzepatide) for type 2 diabetes on 13 May 2022, and the EU authorised it on 15 September 2022. It acts on two hormone receptors, for GLP-1 and GIP.

fda-pcac-2026-vote.title: FDA advisers vote on seven peptides
fda-pcac-2026-vote.text: On 23 July 2026 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8–6, with one abstention, to recommend BPC-157 for the 503A list of substances US pharmacies may compound on prescription; of the seven peptides it considered, it recommended six (BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax and epitalon, but not emideltide, also called DSIP), as reported from the public meeting. The vote is advisory and non-binding and went against FDA staff's own recommendation, so legal compounding stays prohibited until the FDA formally adopts it and completes rulemaking. None of these peptides is an approved medicine in the EU, the UK or the US (Semax is registered as a medicine in Russia), and a listing would not be a marketing authorisation, would say nothing about whether they work, and would change nothing in the EU or the Netherlands.

us-pcac-2026-peptide-vote.title: US advisers back six peptides for pharmacy compounding
us-pcac-2026-peptide-vote.summary: On 23 July 2026 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8 to 6, with one abstention, to recommend BPC-157 for the 503A list of ingredients pharmacies may use. Over two days it considered seven peptides and recommended six: BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax and epitalon, but not emideltide. These results are as reported from the public meeting; the FDA has posted no minutes. The vote is advice only, and went against FDA staff's own proposal. Compounding with these peptides stays prohibited until the FDA adopts the advice and completes rulemaking. None of them is an approved medicine in the EU, the UK or the US (Semax is registered as a medicine in Russia). A listing would let US pharmacies compound them on prescription. It would not be an approval and says nothing about whether they work. Nothing changes in the EU or the Netherlands.
us-pcac-2026-peptide-vote.next: The FDA decides whether to propose a rule, which would then be open for public comment. No date has been set. On 22 October 2026 the Federal Register held no proposed rule.

wada-2027-prohibited-list.title: The 2027 Prohibited List names peptides in section S0
wada-2027-prohibited-list.summary: WADA published the 2027 Prohibited List on 21 September 2026. It takes effect on 1 January 2027. Section S0 now names 'peptides' among its examples, next to BPC-157. WADA says a peptide that the list does not name may still be prohibited. The Dutch Doping Authority will publish its Dutch translation from 1 January 2027.

Removed entries are copied whole (Dutch and Belgian terms for the Dutch glossary); changed entries give the old definition. diarrhoea and constipation were reworded only to avoid the British-only word 'poo' (not European framing); their old text is kept for completeness. clinicaltrials-gov lost a see_also link to 'ctis' (the EU Clinical Trials Information System), which had no glossary entry on English.

flemish-decree.definition: A law passed by the Flemish Parliament, for the Dutch-speaking part of Belgium. In Flanders it has the same force as a national law.

aliases: National Institute for Public Health and the Environment
rivm.definition: The Dutch national institute for public health and the environment. This government institute gives advice on infections, hygiene and vaccines.

thuisarts.definition: A Dutch website with health advice for patients, written by the Dutch College of General Practitioners (NHG).

glossary/final-qa.json.zeranol.definition: A substance that acts like the hormone oestrogen. Some countries outside the EU give it to cattle to make them grow faster; the EU does not allow this.
glossary/final-qa.json.zilpaterol.definition: A substance added to cattle feed in some countries, so that the animals put on more lean meat before slaughter. The EU does not allow it.
glossary/final-qa.json.emideltide.definition: A lab-made copy of a small peptide first described in 1977 as delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP). It is not approved as a medicine in the EU, the UK or the US.
glossary/final-qa.json.plenary-vote.definition: A vote by all members of the European Parliament together. It comes after a committee has worked on the text.
glossary/final-qa.json.diarrhoea.definition: Loose or watery poo, more often than usual. It can make you lose a lot of water.
glossary/final-qa.json.constipation.definition: Pooing less often than usual, or finding it hard to poo.

explainers.json.$comment: Changed on 26 October 2026 by the fact-check of group glossary-ui-media-en: the semaglutide low-blood-sugar explainer said 'call an ambulance'; it now says 'call your local emergency number', as the content brief requires and as its twin glp1-class-hypo already did (not European framing; kept for completeness). The emideltide glossary definition (above) was also widened by the fact-check to 'the US, the UK, Canada or Australia' after database searches; its pre-refocus text is the one archived above.
explainers.json.insulin-glp1-hypo.steps.4: Low sugar signs: sweating, shaking, hunger, confusion. Take sugar now. Can't swallow? Call an ambulance.
explainers.json.insulin-glp1-hypo.summary: On its own, semaglutide rarely makes blood sugar too low. With insulin or a sulfonylurea tablet it can, so the prescriber may lower those doses. Know the signs and take sugar at once. If the person cannot swallow, call an ambulance.
